alt: Assumption 1 (brain, hormones, genetics and evolution explain behaviour) is tested by Dement and Kleitman through brain activity, Hassett et al. through hormones and evolution, and Hölzel et al. through brain structure. Assumption 2 (interaction with other factors) is shown by Hassett et al. (socialisation strengthens a difference) and Hölzel et al. (training changes the brain).
caption: Each study tests a different part of the assumptions.

after: ## Dement and Kleitman (1957): sleep and dreams
alt: Five numbered steps: participants avoided caffeine and alcohol and arrived near bedtime, were connected to an EEG, were woken by a doorbell without being told their sleep stage, reported dreams into a recorder, and in one part estimated whether a dream had lasted five or fifteen minutes.
caption: Standardised waking and reporting made the procedure replicable.

after: ## Dement and Kleitman (1957): sleep and dreams
alt: Bars show 152 of 191 REM awakenings produced a dream report compared with 11 of 160 NREM awakenings, and 92 of 111 five-or-fifteen-minute estimates were correct. Vertical eye movements matched a dream of climbing ladders; horizontal movements matched watching two people throw tomatoes.
caption: Dream reports came mostly from REM, but not only from REM.

after: ## Hassett et al. (2008): monkey toy preferences
alt: Monkeys were given a wheeled toy and a plush toy together and contacts were coded with a behavioural checklist. Illustrative bars show males interacting more with wheeled toys and females more evenly. The conclusion: hormones may contribute to the difference, which socialisation may strengthen.
caption: Males preferred wheeled toys, as boys tend to; females were more even.

after: ## Hölzel et al. (2011): mindfulness and brain scans
alt: Sixteen MBSR participants and seventeen controls had MRI scans and a mindfulness questionnaire before and after eight weeks; only the MBSR group took the programme. Results show increased grey-matter concentration in the left hippocampus and other regions. Strengths and weaknesses of the design follow.
caption: Scanning before and after, with a control group, links the change to the programme.

alt: Two linked cards: the first mark comes from stating the assumption accurately (cognitions explained by the brain); the second from a precise finding tied to it (dream reports far more likely after REM than NREM awakenings). A note warns that a vague claim without a finding earns little.
caption: State the assumption, then tie a precise finding to it.
